we have developed a novel approach to studying persuasion in advance fee fraud, which we believe will have important implications for both the study of persuasion in online communication and the design of automated intervention tools for combating fraud.

we present a new dataset of scam-bait conversations, and we show that the language used by scammers and baiters in these conversations has a number of distinct properties that can be exploited for automated classification.

our work is the first attempt to understand the dynamics of scammer-baiter interactions, to identify scam-baiting communications amidst regular email and to detect the scammer and baiters messages from their conversations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, while the initial solicitation email is a crucial part of the scam, it is only one part, and that understanding how fraudsters persuade victims requires a broader perspective than simply the initial email.

the linguistic patterns we have identified in scam-baiting communications can be used to identify scam-baiting interactions and to identify the role of each participant in a conversation, and that the patterns are likely to be present in other types of online persuasion, such as marketing and social influence.
